analysis.one_liner: Taxes 90-100% of bonuses and stock profits taken by executives of failing banks just before FDIC takeover.
analysis.headline: The bill went no further than a single committee referral: it was introduced with 7 cosponsors, never received a hearing, vote, or floor action, and died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The DEPOSIT Act would amend the tax code so that executives of banks seized by the FDIC pay a 90% tax on bonuses paid by their bank in the 60 days before takeover, and a 100% tax on profits from selling their bank's stock in that same window, if their income was above $250,000. It states the Senate's intent that the money raised go back into the Deposit Insurance Fund, the fund taxpayers stand behind when banks fail. The bill was prompted by the March 2023 bank failures, in which some executives of seized banks had received bonuses and cashed out stock shortly before the government stepped in.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers and the Deposit Insurance Fund. When a bank fails, the FDIC covers insured deposits and the fund can be drawn down, with costs that can fall back on the banking system and, ultimately, the public. This bill would route money clawed back from failing banks' executives into that fund, and would deny executives the benefit of cashing out just before their bank collapses.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Taxpayers behind the deposit insurance fund

how_it_helps.text: Imposes a 90% tax rate on bonuses paid by an insured depository institution within 60 days before the FDIC is appointed conservator or receiver, for executives whose income exceeds $250,000 [S3].
Imposes a 100% tax rate on profits from selling stock of the failing bank within 60 days before FDIC takeover, targeting executives who cash out just before the collapse [S3].
Expresses the sense of the Senate that the revenue raised be returned to the FDIC's Deposit Insurance Fund, which backstops insured deposits [S2] [S3].
Reaches executives of subsidiaries and controlled corporate groups, closing the most obvious structural loopholes in the definition of who counts as an executive officer [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Executives of failed banks who received bonuses or sold bank stock in the two months before FDIC takeover and earned over $250,000. No other taxpayers or industries are directly taxed under the bill.

drawbacks.text: The tax only reaches money moving in a 60-day window before receivership, so executives who took large bonuses or sold stock earlier, before trouble was obvious, would keep it [S3].
A retrospective tax on transactions already completed raises fairness and legal questions, since people arranged their affairs under the old rules.
Taxing bonuses after the fact does not prevent banks from paying them in the first place, and does not address the underlying risk-taking that makes banks fail.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but narrow: the bill applies only to executives of banks already seized by the FDIC and only to bonuses and stock sales in the final two months, so it recovers a slice of the money rather than all of it. The cost falls entirely on a small group of high earners who profited from failing banks, and the revenue is directed to the fund that absorbs the damage. An honest supporter would acknowledge the design is reactive and limited rather than a broad fix for bank executive pay.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Finance Committee never acted on the bill after referring it, and it expired when the 118th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Blumenthal introduced the bill on March 14, 2023, in the days after the FDIC seized Silicon Valley Bank and Signature Bank, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance the same day [S1] [S5].
Seven senators cosponsored the bill, six Democrats and one Independent; no Republican cosponsored [S4].
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action ever followed the referral; the action history ends on the day of introduction [S5].
The bill died at the end of the 118th Congress on January 3, 2025, without ever receiving a vote in either chamber [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Executives of failed banks who received bonuses or sold bank stock shortly before FDIC takeover kept that money with no additional tax, and the Deposit Insurance Fund received none of the clawed-back revenue.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so there is no roll call to read; all seven cosponsors were Democrats or Independents and no Republican signed on, suggesting one-sided but shallow support.

industries.note: The bill would tax away 90-100% of bonuses and stock-sale profits taken in the 60 days before FDIC takeover by executives earning over $250,000. Those executives kept the money because the bill never advanced.

industries.industry: Banking industry and deposit insurance fund
industries.note: Revenue would flow into the FDIC's Deposit Insurance Fund, which all insured banks help capitalize, slightly offsetting losses when banks fail. The tax applies only to seized banks' executives, not to the industry broadly.
